section_summary: This section covers U.S. State Department correspondence, consular despatches, and military intelligence reports from late 1940 to early 1941 concerning Japan's internal political reorganization and external expansion. It documents the establishment of the 'New Structure' (Shintaisei) and the Imperial Rule Assistance Association under Prime Minister Prince Fumimaro Konoe, highlighting wide-ranging social regimentation, rationing, the dissolution of political parties, and the military's constitutional independence from cabinet control. The documents also include an extensive intelligence report from Batavia on Japanese aggressive tactics in China and ambitions toward the Netherlands East Indies, diplomatic reporting from Vichy on potential cabinet instability in Tokyo and Soviet-Japanese pact talks, and the creation of the Foreign Office's South Seas Bureau to advance the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere.

subfiles.about: Press survey of Japanese newspaper reports illustrating the social, economic, and religious regimentation imposed under the New Structure.
subfiles.summary: Clippings detail New Structure regimentation: uniforms, luxury/travel curbs, dissolved Rotary/labor/Christian groups, rationing, price-fixing penalties, Kagawa's arrest, and anti-espionage vigilance.
subfiles.title: Press Excerpts on the Impact of the New Structure on Japanese Daily Life, Religion, and Labor

subfiles.about: Consular despatch transmitting a comprehensive intelligence memorandum by Dutch officer J. N. Heijbroek assessing Japanese psychological traits, military misconduct in China, and southward expansionism.
subfiles.summary: American Consul General Walter A. Foote forwards an extensive memorandum prepared for Netherlands Indies authorities by Sub-Lieutenant J. N. Heijbroek, a Dutch language officer and former commercial agent with 19 years of residence in Japan and China. Heijbroek delivers a biting assessment of Japanese national psychology, commercial unreliability, and military conduct, asserting that Japanese leadership respects only decisive strength and uses deceit, terror, and bribery as standard operating methods. Drawing on observations from the war in China—including widespread corruption and blockade abuses at Tientsin, economic exploitation in Manchuria, and the use of poison gas around Wuhan—he warns that Japan's military and naval factions are actively preparing to strike southward against the Netherlands East Indies for oil and raw materials, urging Western democracies to present an unyielding united front.
subfiles.title: Despatch Transmitting Memorandum 'A Few Observations Concerning Japan, Based on the Varied Experiences of a 19 Year Stay in Japan and China'

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing Embassy Tokyo's Despatch No. 5106 and Hugh Byas's study on Japan's New Structure.
subfiles.summary: Fales summarizes Byas's monograph on the New Structure as a fascist reorganization from China-war stalemate, detailing IRAA mechanisms and the Army's refusal to cede independence from the Emperor.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 5106 ('The New Structure in Japan')

subfiles.about: Embassy despatch transmitting an authoritative monograph by journalist Hugh Byas analyzing Japan's New Structure and corporative state design.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits a study by Hugh Byas, Tokyo correspondent for The New York Times and The Times, evaluating the origins and structures of Japan's New National Structure. Byas explains that Prince Fumimaro Konoe launched the movement because Japan's military stalemate in China necessitated total national mobilization and a high-degree national defense state. The study describes the twin machinery of the Imperial Rule Assistance Movement (executive bureaucracy guiding the people from above) and Association (popular cooperative councils reporting upward), contrasting Japanese Emperor-centric totalitarianism with Italian Fascism while emphasizing that the Imperial Japanese Army's refusal to integrate into the cabinet preserves Japan's longstanding constitutional dualism.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 5106: 'The New Structure in Japan' Enclosing Study by Hugh Byas

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting French diplomatic observations on political instability in Tokyo and inquiring about Soviet aid to China and a Russo-Japanese pact.
subfiles.summary: Matthews relays Chauvel citing Arsène-Henry's report of Tokyo nervousness and possible Konoe collapse, asking whether Soviet China aid ceased or a Soviet-Japanese pact was near.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1039 from Vichy (Sections 1 and 2) Regarding Japanese Internal Situation and Soviet Policy

subfiles.about: Diplomatic telegram providing Washington's assessment of continuing Soviet military aid to China and the status of Soviet-Japanese negotiations.
subfiles.summary: Hull tells Vichy to doubt claims Soviet China aid ceased, expecting it to increase, while Soviet-Japanese pact talks continue amid substantial obstacles.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 798 to American Embassy, Vichy, Regarding Soviet Aid to China and Soviet-Japanese Talks

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing Tokyo Military Attaché Report No. 10,242 on Japanese domestic developments and foreign relations.
subfiles.summary: Fales reviews a November 1940 intelligence report on IRAA criticism, a new Foreign Office South Seas Bureau, a 12.3% rice-crop drop, imperial anniversary events, and Indochina pressure.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Military Intelligence Report No. 10,242

subfiles.about: Military intelligence report reviewing Japanese domestic developments under the New Structure and analyzing foreign policy toward the South Seas, U.S., U.S.S.R., Thailand, and Indochina.
subfiles.summary: The U.S. Military Attaché in Tokyo presents a comprehensive review of Japanese domestic and foreign developments in late 1940. Domestically, the report examines press criticisms regarding bureaucratic sluggishness, lack of direction, and high projected budgets within the Imperial Rule Assistance Association, the reorganization of the Foreign Office's South Seas Bureau to advance the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere, a severe decline in the rice harvest, and the Emperor's 2,600th imperial anniversary festivities. Internationally, it assesses Japanese press attitudes toward Franklin D. Roosevelt's re-election, anxieties concerning Soviet alignment with the Anglo-American democracies versus the Axis, rumors of an Anglo-American-Thai alliance, and continued Japanese military encroachment in French Indochina.
subfiles.title: Military Attaché Report No. 10,242: 'Comments on Current Events - No. 38'
